messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 65

He is a 63-year-old Oceania man who has spent most of his adult life working as a financial analyst, a role that has trained him to be precise, measured, and in control of what can be predicted. He describes himself as someone who has always taken pride in staying calm under pressure, keeping numbers organized, and thinking several steps ahead. That way of moving through the world changes in an instant after a life-threatening accident that happens while he is traveling home from work.

He recalls the accident in fragments at first: the sudden sound, the violent jolt, the sensation of time slowing and then breaking apart. In the moment, he is certain he is going to die. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. He feels his chest tighten, his breathing become shallow, and his hands brace against the force of impact. Afterward, when the scene is over and he is alive, he is struck less by relief than by disbelief. He keeps thinking that surviving feels impossible, almost like a clerical error in the universe. In the first days and weeks, he moves through the world as if part of him is still back at the site of the accident, waiting for the next blow.

At home, his wife notices that he is no longer the same man who used to unpack his briefcase, ask about her day, and settle into the evening with newspaper or spreadsheets. He becomes jumpy at sudden noises, especially metal scraping, tires screeching, or a loud bang from the kitchen. He startles hard enough that she worries he will fall. He begins checking doors and windows more often, then checking them again. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants and insists on knowing the route everywhere they go. He tells himself this is simply prudence, but he cannot ignore how exhausted he feels by the end of ordinary errands.

Sleep becomes one of the hardest parts. He falls asleep reluctantly and wakes in the night with his heart racing, often after dreams that recreate the accident without warning. Some nights he wakes drenched in sweat, certain for a moment that he is still trapped inside the vehicle, smelling smoke or rubber, hearing the noise in his head. When he wakes, he lies very still so he does not alarm his wife, though inside he feels panicked and ashamed. He starts leaving a lamp on and avoids going back to sleep immediately because he dreads returning to the same dream.

During the day, reminders of the accident intrude on him in ways he cannot control. A siren in the distance, a report of a collision on the radio, or even a particular stretch of road can pull him back so completely that he feels the physical sensation of the event all over again. His thoughts race: if he had left earlier, if he had taken another route, if he had been more alert. He spends long periods replaying the lead-up to the accident, trying to identify a moment when he might have prevented it. Because his work has always rewarded careful analysis, he is especially trapped by the need to explain what happened. The effort only deepens his frustration when no amount of reasoning makes him feel safe.

He begins avoiding driving whenever he can. At first he makes excuses, asking his wife to drive or choosing to work from home more often. Then he avoids the roads near the accident entirely, even if the detour is inconvenient. He notices that his world is shrinking around this avoidance. He declines invitations, leaves gatherings early, and becomes less present with family because he is constantly scanning for exits and dangers. His wife says he seems distant, and he knows she is right. He is physically there but often elsewhere, caught in his own vigilance. At times he feels a flatness he cannot explain, a sense that he is watching his life from a distance rather than living it.

He is embarrassed by how much the accident still controls him. He has spent decades making decisions for other people, assessing risk, and maintaining a composed exterior. Now he struggles to trust his own body. He notices irritability where patience used to be, and a fatigue that lingers even on days when he has done very little. Still, he continues to show up to work, where he can lose himself for a few hours in reports, projections, and familiar routines. He functions best when the world is orderly and numbers behave as expected, but even there he remains tense, as if one wrong sound might send him back to that moment on the road.

Over time, he begins to speak about the accident more clearly, though still with effort. He describes not only what happened but the way it has changed the texture of ordinary life: how his body now reacts before his mind can intervene, how sleep feels unsafe, how the future has become narrower and more carefully managed. He is aware that the accident is over, yet his nervous system behaves as if danger is still present.
